sections.content: One of the biggest debates in real estate investing right now is simple: Airbnb vs long term rental — which makes more money? The honest answer is that it depends on your property, your market, and how much work you want to put in. But there IS a clear winner for most investors once you run the real numbers. If you're just getting started with rental properties, check out our [Rental Property Investing for Beginners: Complete Guide](aiwholesail.com/guides/rental-property-investing-guide) before diving in. This article will walk you through a direct, numbers-based comparison so you can make the right call for your situation.
The Basic Income Difference: Short Term vs Long Term Rentals

On the surface, short-term rentals (STRs) like Airbnb look like a no-brainer. A property that rents for $1,500 per month as a long-term rental might command $150 to $200 per night on Airbnb. If you get even 15 nights of bookings per month, that's $2,250 to $3,000 — a 50% to 100% premium over traditional renting. In tourist-heavy markets like Phoenix, Atlanta, or Dallas, strong occupancy rates can push those numbers even higher. Check out active deal data for [Phoenix](aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az), [Atlanta](aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), and [Dallas](aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx) to see what properties are currently available in these high-demand rental markets.
'Gross revenue is vanity, net income is sanity.' — Every experienced real estate investor who has compared Airbnb to long-term rentals after doing the math.
The Real Costs of Running an Airbnb

Here's where many new investors get surprised. Airbnb income looks great on the top line, but the expenses are significantly higher than long-term rentals. Before you compare the two strategies, you need to understand what actually eats into your short-term rental revenue.

items: Cleaning fees and turnovers: $75 to $200 per guest checkout, multiple times per month
Furnishing the property: $5,000 to $20,000 upfront to furnish a full home
Airbnb platform fees: typically 3% of each booking
Higher utility costs: you pay electric, water, WiFi, and streaming services
Supplies and consumables: toiletries, paper towels, coffee, soap — these add up fast
Property management (if outsourced): 20% to 35% of gross revenue for STR managers
Higher wear and tear: more frequent guest turnover means more repairs and replacements
Vacancy risk: an empty week means zero income, no guaranteed rent check

sections.content: Side-by-Side Example: $250,000 Property in a Mid-Size City

Let's use a real-world example to see which strategy wins. Take a 3-bedroom home purchased for $250,000 in a mid-size city. As a long-term rental, it rents for $1,600 per month. After mortgage, taxes, insurance, and a 10% vacancy and maintenance reserve, you net roughly $350 to $500 per month in cash flow. As an Airbnb, that same home generates $2,800 per month in gross revenue at 70% occupancy and $150 per night. Subtract cleaning fees ($400), supplies ($100), utilities ($200), platform fees ($85), and a property manager at 25% ($700), and your net drops to around $1,315 per month. That's still more than the long-term rental — but only if occupancy holds. Drop to 50% occupancy and your net falls below $800, making the extra effort questionable. Use our free [Cash Flow Calculator](aiwholesail.com/tools/cash-flow-calculator) to run these numbers for your own property before you commit to either strategy.

Pro Tip: Before choosing short-term rental, check your city's STR regulations. Many cities like New York, Denver, and Santa Monica require permits or have banned STRs in certain zones entirely. A property that can't legally operate as an Airbnb is a long-term rental by default.
When Airbnb Wins

Airbnb outperforms long-term rentals in specific situations. If your property is near a major tourist attraction, convention center, beach, ski resort, or university, demand will be consistent and nightly rates will be strong. Markets like Scottsdale (Phoenix metro), Nashville, and Savannah regularly see STR investors double or even triple their long-term rental income. Airbnb also wins if you plan to use the property yourself. A vacation home that sits empty part of the year can offset its carrying costs by renting out the weeks you're not there — a strategy similar to [house hacking](aiwholesail.com/blog/house-hacking-live-free), where you use your property to eliminate or reduce your own housing costs.
When Long-Term Rentals Win

For most investors — especially those building a portfolio — long-term rentals offer something Airbnb can't easily deliver: predictability. A signed 12-month lease means 12 months of guaranteed income, no nightly turnover stress, and far lower management overhead. Long-term rentals are also easier to scale. Managing 10 long-term rentals is far more manageable than managing 10 Airbnb units, which can feel like running a small hotel. If you're exploring other ways to maximize returns on residential rentals, you might also look at [Section 8 rental investing](aiwholesail.com/blog/section-8-rental-investing), which offers guaranteed government-backed rent payments and lower vacancy risk.
The Hybrid Approach: Best of Both Worlds?

Some savvy investors use a hybrid model — running the property as an Airbnb during peak season (summer, holidays, major events) and switching to a medium-term rental (30+ day stays on Furnished Finder or VRBO) during slower months. This strategy smooths out income without the volatility of nightly bookings year-round. Medium-term rentals to traveling nurses, remote workers, or corporate clients can generate $2,000 to $3,500 per month with far lower turnover costs than traditional Airbnb. It's a middle ground worth exploring if your market has clear seasonality.
Property Type Matters Too

The type of property you own affects which strategy makes more sense. A single-family home in a suburban neighborhood typically performs better as a long-term rental because families want to settle in and put down roots. A condo near a downtown or waterfront area may command excellent Airbnb rates. Multifamily properties — duplexes, triplexes, and quads — offer another angle entirely, since you can live in one unit and rent the others. If you're deciding between property types, read our breakdown of [single family vs multifamily](aiwholesail.com/blog/single-family-vs-multifamily) to understand which fits your investment goals. And if you're using a strategy like the BRRRR method to fund future purchases, long-term rental income provides the stable cash flow lenders want to see — learn more in our [BRRRR Method guide](aiwholesail.com/guides/brrrr-method-explained).

Pro Tip: Run your numbers at 50% occupancy before committing to Airbnb. If the deal doesn't work at half occupancy, the risk is too high. Markets change, regulations shift, and a slow month can wipe out weeks of profit.
The Verdict: Which Strategy Makes More Money?

In the right market, Airbnb can generate 1.5x to 2.5x more gross income than a long-term rental. But after expenses, active management, and the reality of vacancy, the net difference often narrows to 20% to 50% more — and that premium comes with significantly more work and risk. Long-term rentals win on simplicity, scalability, and financing friendliness. Airbnb wins on income potential in high-demand tourist or event markets where occupancy stays above 65%. The best investors don't ask 'which is better?' in the abstract — they run the numbers for their specific property and market before deciding.
